intro: New York City runs a government registry for this: the Parks Department's Great Trees of New York City list, started in 1985 and expanded in 2024 after a nomination drive drew more than 270 submissions. Most trees here carry that designation; the rest earned their place another way, like a magnolia that is a city landmark and a pear that came out of Ground Zero alive. The five boroughs each hold at least one. Some are colonial-era survivors; one was planted so a park would have something to be famous for.
meta_description: NYC runs an official Great Trees registry. Meet a 300-year-old Greenwich Village elm, a wild tulip tree older than the city itself, and twenty-five more.
question_answer: New York City's oldest tree is very likely the Queens Giant, a tulip tree in Alley Pond Park estimated between 350 and 450 years old by different measures, old enough to predate the Dutch colony of New Amsterdam entirely. It stands in a wooded section of the park in eastern Queens, reachable on foot from the Douglaston Long Island Rail Road station.
question_meta: NYC's oldest tree is likely the Queens Giant, a 350-450 year old tulip tree in Alley Pond Park. Its story, exact location, and 26 more trees.
question_context: The Queens Giant's claim to being New York City's oldest living thing rests on measurement rather than legend. At 133.8 feet, it is the tallest carefully measured tree in the five boroughs, and tulip trees of that height in undisturbed forest are reliably centuries old; the New York City Parks Department states it is at least 368 years old, while some arborists place the range as wide as 350 to 450. Either figure puts its germination before the 1664 English takeover of New Amsterdam, and some local accounts connect trees in this stretch of Alley Pond Park to 17th century land dealings between the Dutch West India Company and the Matinecock people who lived here first, though no source ties this specific trunk to a documented transaction. What is not in question is that it has spent its entire life essentially unmanaged, growing in what is now protected forest rather than a planted garden, which is rare enough in New York that the Parks Department calls it possibly the oldest living organism in the metropolitan area. Getting there: Douglaston station on the LIRR Port Washington line, then a short walk into Alley Pond Park's wooded trails.

faq.q: What is the oldest tree in New York City?
faq.a: Likely the Queens Giant, a wild tulip tree in Alley Pond Park estimated at 350 to 450 years old, old enough to predate the English takeover of New Amsterdam in 1664.

faq.q: Where is the best place to see old trees in New York City?
faq.a: No single spot has a monopoly. The Thain Family Forest at the New York Botanical Garden in the Bronx is the largest surviving patch of the city's original woodland, but Central Park, Prospect Park and several borough parks each hold at least one Great Tree of their own.

faq.q: Are New York City's Great Trees free to see?
faq.a: Twenty-three of the twenty-seven stand in free public parks or cemeteries. The New York Botanical Garden charges general admission to its grounds, but the Thain Family Forest tree is within that same free-to-walk woodland once inside.

faq.q: How does a tree become an official Great Tree of New York City?
faq.a: Through public nomination to the Parks Department. The original 1985 list came from citizen submissions for unusual size, rare species, striking form or historical significance, and a 2023-2024 nomination drive that drew over 270 submissions added 61 more trees to the roughly 65 that had survived from the original round.

trees.name: The Hangman's Elm

location.address: Northwest corner, Washington Square Park, New York, NY 10012

trees.story: This elm is one of the oldest living things on Manhattan Island, and almost everything colorful ever said about it is unproven. Its nickname comes from a folk legend that traitors and criminals were hanged from its branches during and after the American Revolution, a story with no supporting court or newspaper record; the earliest known references to it as a hanging tree only appear in print in the late 19th century, generations after the events they describe. What is documented is its age: the New York City Parks Department measured it at 310 years old in 1989, later revising that to a more cautious more than 300 years, with some accounts pushing the figure to 346. It stands at the northwest corner of Washington Square, a plot of land that served as a potter's field and public execution ground in the early 1800s, close enough to the tree that a real 1820 hanging nearby, of Rose Butler for arson, may be the seed of fact the legend grew from. The tree survived a 2012 park renovation that construction crews came close to damaging.
trees.transport: West 4th Street (Metro A/B/C/D/E/F/M), 3 min walk
trees.notes: Age given as a range (300-346 years) because sources genuinely disagree, from NYC Parks' cautious 'more than 300 years' to a commonly cited 346. Pin confirmed 2026-07-27: OpenStreetMap carries a contributor-mapped, survey-sourced node named "Hangman's Elm" (species Ulmus procera, planted 1679, matching this entry's high-end age estimate of 346 years almost exactly), a few metres from the existing estimate.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it as one of the oldest trees on Manhattan, standing at the northwest corner of the park. It stands at Washington Square Park.

trees.name: The Black Tupelo of the Ramble

location.address: The Ramble, near West 78th Street, Central Park, New York, NY 10024

trees.story: Central Park has two competing claimants for its oldest tree, and this one has the better paperwork. A London plane near the Reservoir might date to 1862, when the Reservoir itself was excavated, but this black tupelo in the Ramble, the deliberately wild, maze-like woodland Frederick Law Olmsted and Calvert Vaux designed into the park's plan, has documentation placing its planting at 1858, four years earlier, during the park's original construction. Black tupelos are native to eastern North American wetlands and swamps, not the schist bedrock Central Park sits on, which makes this a planted specimen rather than a survivor of the farmland and settlements the park displaced. The species is prized by ecologists for its brilliant, early scarlet fall color and by foresters for its resistance to rot, qualities that have let this tree outlast most of the park's original 1850s plantings. It stands in one of the Ramble's quieter, less trafficked paths, a 19th century engineering project that has spent a century and a half looking convincingly unplanned.
trees.transport: 81st Street-Museum of Natural History (Metro B/C), 8 min walk
trees.notes: Coordinates are an estimate for the Ramble near West 78th Street; no surveyed point for the specific tree was found.

best_time.label: late September into October, often the first tree in the Ramble to turn, in brilliant scarlet

trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the fall colour, scarlet and early, on a swamp tree growing where the park is bedrock. It stands on one of the Ramble's quieter, less trafficked paths.

trees.name: The Camperdown Elm

location.address: Near the Boathouse, Prospect Park, Brooklyn, NY 11225

trees.story: Every Camperdown elm on Earth is a clone, and this one is among the oldest. The cultivar began in the 1830s when a gardener for the Earl of Camperdown found a single mutant elm branch, contorted and weeping instead of growing upright, on the Camperdown House estate near Dundee, Scotland. Because the mutation cannot be grown from seed, every specimen since has been propagated by grafting a cutting onto a straight-trunked host, which makes each Camperdown elm in the world a genetic twin of that one Scottish branch. This graft was planted near Prospect Park's Boathouse in 1872, a gift to the young park, and by the 1960s had declined badly enough that Brooklyn nearly lost it, until the poet Marianne Moore, a devoted Prospect Park visitor, wrote publicly in its defense and helped rally the conservation campaign that saved it. She later called it Brooklyn's crowning curio. Its low, twisted canopy, propped and cabled for support, still spreads wide enough that visitors duck to walk beneath it, a shape no other tree in the park shares by nature.
trees.transport: Prospect Park (Metro B/Q/S), 10 min walk
trees.notes: Pin corrected 2026-07-27 (about 70m): OpenStreetMap carries a contributor-mapped, survey-sourced node named "Camperdown Elm" (species Ulmus glabra 'Camperdownii', planted 1872, matching this entry's own planting year exactly), replacing the previous Boathouse-area estimate. Photo URL fixed 2026-07-28: the stored thumb path (commons/thumb/e/e0/...) 404'd, caught by a site-wide hash-path check against Commons' API; the real current path is 2/20. Fetched and viewed directly to confirm it's still the same weeping, umbrella-canopied elm before swapping.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by its low, twisted, weeping canopy, propped and cabled, spreading wide enough that you duck to walk beneath it. It stands near the Boathouse in Prospect Park, Brooklyn.

trees.name: The Sassafras of Green-Wood

location.address: Green-Wood Cemetery, 500 25th Street, Brooklyn, NY 11232

trees.story: Green-Wood Cemetery has counted this as its oldest tree, possibly older than the cemetery itself, which was founded in 1838 on rolling glacial hills chosen specifically because the terrain already supported mature, established woodland. Sassafras trees rarely reach the size or age this specimen has, since the species usually grows as a smaller understory tree that spreads through root suckers rather than living to great individual age; this one, or rather these two, since it appears as a pair of trunks a few feet apart, may be the last survivors of a larger colonial root system that once covered more ground. Nobody has cored the tree to confirm an exact age, and Green-Wood's own arborists are candid that the favorable growing conditions inside a manicured 478 acre cemetery likely inflate its size relative to a wild sassafras of the same age, making size an unreliable proxy for years here. What is certain is that it predates most of the 600,000 people buried around it, a rare case of a cemetery's oldest resident having no grave at all.
trees.access: Free, cemetery open daily (check seasonal hours)
trees.transport: 25th Street (Metro R), at the cemetery gate
trees.notes: Age is explicitly uncertain in the source material itself (Green-Wood's own write-up says there is no way to confirm age without coring the tree, and cautions that cemetery growing conditions likely make the tree larger than its age alone would suggest). Coordinates are for the cemetery's main entrance, not a surveyed point for the tree's specific location inside the grounds. Photo viewed directly: two large old trees a few feet apart in the cemetery, headstones visible, an exact match to the story's own description of the tree appearing as a pair of trunks.

best_time.label: October, when its leaves turn a mix of yellow, orange and purple, sometimes all on the same branch

trees.verify_notes: Green-Wood's own great-trees page has gone 404 since it was cited; repointed to the Internet Archive snapshot of the same page rather than dropping the citation. The cemetery's indexed text places this tree in Section 54, between Forest and Locust Avenues, west of Cedar Dell, which is more precise than our current gate-level pin and is the obvious upgrade when somebody geocodes it.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by its pair of trunks standing a few feet apart, likely survivors of one older root system. It stands in Green-Wood Cemetery, Brooklyn.

trees.name: The Queens Giant

location.address: Alley Pond Park, near Alley Creek, Douglaston, Queens, NY 11364

trees.story: This tree was already centuries old when New Amsterdam was still a Dutch trading post, and unlike almost everything else on this list, nobody planted it. At 133.8 feet the Queens Giant is the tallest carefully measured tree in New York City, a tulip poplar growing wild in a stretch of Alley Pond Park's forest that has never been cleared, and the New York City Parks Department dates it to at least 368 years old, with other estimates ranging as wide as 350 to 450. Tulip trees can live 600 years and reach over 150 feet under ideal conditions, and this specimen's height alone marks it as one of the oldest living things in the entire New York metropolitan region, likely older than any building, monument or institution in the five boroughs. Some local histories connect the surrounding land to 17th century transactions between the Dutch West India Company and the Matinecock people who lived here before European settlement, though no source confirms this specific tree witnessed any documented exchange. It has simply kept growing, in a park most of the city drives past on the Long Island Expressway without knowing it is there.
trees.transport: Douglaston (LIRR Port Washington line), 10 min walk
trees.notes: Coordinates taken directly from the confirmed photo's embedded GPS metadata (40°45'10.8"N, 73°44'49.2"W), a rare case of a precisely surveyed point for the tree itself rather than an estimate. Photo URL fixed 2026-07-28: the stored path (commons/e/ef/...) 404'd, caught by the same site-wide hash-path check that found Madrid's and the Camperdown Elm's broken links; the real current path is 6/67. Fetched and viewed directly (a tall bare-branched tree towering above its neighbours in a leaf-litter forest) to confirm it's still the same tree before swapping.

best_time.label: October, when its canopy turns a luminous golden yellow

trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by its height, 133.8 feet, the tallest carefully measured tree in New York City, rising from uncleared forest. It stands in Alley Pond Park, Queens.

trees.name: The Manchurian Linden of Kissena Park

location.address: Kissena Park, near the tennis courts, Flushing, Queens, NY 11355

trees.story: This linden is a leftover from a 19th century nursery business rather than a park planting, standing 75 feet north of a restroom next to Kissena Park's tennis courts on land that was once part of Samuel Bowne Parsons's commercial tree nursery. Parsons, whose family also planted Manhattan's Hangman's Elm-era Washington Square trees and much of Central Park's original stock, ran one of the era's most important import operations from this site starting in the 1870s, bringing Japanese maples to America for the first time and propagating rhododendrons at commercial scale. After Parsons died in 1906, the city absorbed part of his former grove into what became Kissena Park, and this Manchurian linden, a species native to forests spanning China, Korea and Russia's far east, is one of more than 100 imported tree varieties that trace back to the original nursery grounds still growing in the park today. It carries Great Tree status as a living fragment of Flushing's forgotten reputation as America's premier 19th century horticultural center, a history most visitors to the tennis courts beside it have no reason to suspect.
trees.transport: Kissena Park, Queens Q17/Q25/Q34 bus, 5 min walk
trees.notes: No source gives a specific planting date for this individual tree; age is estimated from the nursery's known 1870s-1900s active period. Pin corrected 2026-07-29 (about 387m, from a park-wide estimate near the tennis courts): NYC Parks' own Great Trees page links this entry to NYC Tree Map ID 5342202, whose record in the Forestry Tree Points open dataset gives an exact point; an independent iNaturalist observation identified as Tilia mandshurica sits about 6m from that same point, two independent sources converging. Worth flagging: the city's own Forestry Tree Points dataset mislabels this record's species as "Tilia cordata" (littleleaf linden), which conflicts with both NYC Parks' own Great Trees text and the iNaturalist identification, both of which agree on Manchurian Linden; treated as a City GIS species-code error rather than evidence this is the wrong tree, since the location link and DBH context still line up.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by standing alone 75 feet north of the restroom beside the tennis courts, a leftover from a 19th century tree nursery. It stands in Kissena Park, Flushing, Queens.

trees.name: The Clove Lakes Colossus

location.address: Clove Lakes Park, north end near the paved path off Forest Avenue, Staten Island, NY 10301

trees.story: Staten Island's tallest tree stands 119 feet, more than 14 feet shorter than Queens' record-holding tulip tree, but old enough on its own terms to anchor the north end of Clove Lakes Park, easily found along a paved path where its trunk, 21.4 feet around, dwarfs everything nearby. Tulip trees like this one are among the tallest native hardwoods in eastern North America, capable of shooting straight up through a forest canopy in search of light rather than spreading wide the way an open-grown oak would, which is part of why the species so often produces the height records claimed on lists like this one. Clove Lakes Park itself preserves one of Staten Island's last stretches of the mixed hardwood forest that once covered most of the borough before 20th century development, and the Colossus, reported at well over 300 years old, would have been an established mature tree when the surrounding land was still farmland rather than parkland. It remains one of Staten Island's contributions to New York City's official Great Trees registry, one of ten entries from the least visited of the five boroughs.
trees.transport: Staten Island Railway to Clove Road area, or S61/S62 bus, 10 min walk
trees.notes: Sourcing for this specific tree is thinner than the others on this list: the height and circumference figures come from secondary coverage rather than a dedicated NYC Parks Great Trees entry found in this search. Age presented as a wide range and the tree flagged for a stronger primary source in a future pass. Location resolved 2026-07-27 via NYC Open Data's Forestry Tree Points dataset: the only Liriodendron tulipifera record citywide with a 93-inch DBH, an exact match to the Colossus's own reported circumference, sitting right at the park's mapped northern boundary off Forest Avenue. An independent iNaturalist observation of the same species sits about 10m away, corroborating the point rather than just the park. Re-confirmed 2026-07-29: NYC Parks' own Great Trees page for this specific listing (great-trees/62) links directly to the same Tree Map objectid this pin was already built on, closing the loop with an official source rather than just a DBH-matching inference.

best_time.label: October, when its canopy turns golden yellow

trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by its trunk, 21.4 feet around, dwarfing everything nearby along the paved path. It stands at the north end of Clove Lakes Park, Staten Island.

trees.name: The Yew of Hero Park

location.address: Hero Park, Victory Boulevard and Louis Street, Staten Island, NY 10301

trees.story: This yew is one of 144 evergreens planted in 1920 around a glacial boulder called Sugar Loaf Rock, each tree standing as a living memorial to a Staten Island resident killed in the First World War. A plaque at the boulder names every soldier the grove commemorates, making Hero Park one of the more literal war memorials in New York City: not statues or a wall of names alone, but a planted forest where each individual tree corresponds to an individual death, a practice with a documented precedent in similar WWI memorial tree plantings elsewhere in the country around the same period. European yews are exceptionally long lived and slow growing, a species choice that all but guaranteed this planting would still be standing a century later, evergreen through every winter since 1920 the way the soldiers it honors never got to see. At just over a century old it is younger than most other trees on this list, but its age is not really the point; the grove was planted to hold a specific memory in place, and a century on, it still does.
trees.transport: S61/S62 bus to Victory Boulevard, at the park
trees.notes: Pin corrected 2026-07-28 (about 1.4km, from a street-corner estimate) via NYC's Forestry Tree Points dataset, using a 48-inch-DBH outlier as the reasoning (every other citywide yew topped out in the teens and 20s). Corrected again 2026-07-29, about 46m: NYC Parks' own Great Trees page for this exact entry (nycgovparks.org/facilities/great-trees/121) links directly to NYC Tree Map ID 5095477, a 17-inch DBH yew at a slightly different point within the same memorial grove. Preferred this over the previous DBH-outlier inference because it is a direct, official Great-Trees-to-Tree-Map linkage for this specific listing rather than a size-based guess; the grove holds 144 yews of varying size, so DBH alone was never a reliable way to single one out. Two Commons photos of the park entrance (CC BY 4.0 and CC BY-SA 3.0, both Jim.henderson) were found and viewed directly but declined as this tree's photo: both show the park's general tree line from Victory Boulevard, not this specific yew isolated from the other 143 memorial evergreens.

best_time.label: August to October: red arils on female trees, the only part that is not poisonous

trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it as one of 144 evergreens planted around the glacial boulder called Sugar Loaf Rock, each marking a fallen soldier. It stands in Hero Park, Staten Island.

trees.name: The Red Oak of the Thain Family Forest

best_time.label: late October, when its leaves turn the deep oxidised red the species is named for, inside forest that predates the city around it

location.address: New York Botanical Garden, 2900 Southern Boulevard, Bronx, NY 10458

trees.story: This oak grows in the middle of the Spicebush Trail inside the Thain Family Forest, a 50 acre stretch of the New York Botanical Garden that has never been logged and represents the largest surviving remnant of the woodland that once covered most of New York City before European colonization. The Botanical Garden was deliberately sited here in 1895 specifically because this forest already existed, a decision that preserved a functioning fragment of pre-colonial Lenapehoking rather than planting a garden from scratch. At a trunk diameter over five feet, this red oak, designated a Great Tree in 2024, ranks among the largest and most accessible specimens in a forest that also holds tulip trees, sweetgums, hemlocks and beeches estimated at up to 300 years old in less visited sections. Red oaks support more moth and butterfly species as larval hosts than almost any other tree genus in the northeastern United States, more than 400 by some counts, making this single oak a small ecosystem of its own even before accounting for its age or size.
trees.access: Paid entry to the New York Botanical Garden: All-Garden Pass adult $35 weekdays, $39 weekends; a Grounds Access Pass at $15 exists for NYC residents with proof of residency. Open 10 a.m. to 6 p.m., Tuesday to Sunday and Monday federal holidays.
trees.transport: Metro-North Harlem Line to Botanical Garden station, at the Mosholu entrance
trees.notes: Coordinates are for the Botanical Garden's main entrance; the tree's specific position on the Spicebush Trail within the 50-acre forest is not separately surveyed.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the trunk, over five feet through, the largest specimen you will pass in the forest. It stands in the middle of the Spicebush Trail in the Thain Family Forest.

trees.name: The Red Horse Chestnut of Van Cortlandt House

best_time.label: May, when its pink flower spikes stand out against the ordinary white-flowering chestnuts nearby

location.address: Van Cortlandt House Museum, Broadway and West 246th Street, Bronx, NY 10471

trees.story: This tree grows on the east lawn of the Van Cortlandt House, built in 1748 and the oldest building still standing in the Bronx, and local tradition holds that a member of the Van Cortlandt family planted it themselves, though no source confirms exactly when. Red horse chestnuts are themselves a hybrid, a cross between the European horse chestnut and a red-flowered American buckeye species, bred for ornamental gardens rather than found in the wild, which means whoever planted this one chose it deliberately for its spring flowers rather than letting it seed in naturally. At nearly 88 feet tall with a trunk over three feet across, it has grown large enough to be one of three horse chestnuts at the house included in the NYC Parks Great Trees registry, all three now part of a Great Tree Clone Program in which cuttings are propagated and planted at new sites around the city, extending the genetic line of trees like this one even as the originals eventually age out. Van Cortlandt House operated as a Revolutionary War-era headquarters at times for both American and British forces, meaning this tree, whatever its precise age, grows on ground that has seen the city's founding conflict up close.
trees.access: Free to view from the park; paid entry to enter the Van Cortlandt House Museum itself
trees.transport: Van Cortlandt Park-242nd Street (Metro 1), 10 min walk
trees.notes: No source gives a specific planting date; NYC Parks itself only states the tree is 'believed' to have been planted by a Van Cortlandt family member, making it 'over a century old.' Age range left wide to reflect that genuine uncertainty. Pin corrected 2026-07-29, about 72m: NYC Parks' own Great Trees page for this entry links to NYC Tree Map ID 5081918, a 42-inch DBH Aesculus x carnea (matching this story's 'trunk over three feet across') at this point. Some residual ambiguity remains honestly noted: NYC Parks' own reporting mentions three horse chestnuts on the house's east lawn, so this is specifically the one the registry tagged for this listing, not necessarily the only one a visitor might notice first.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by its size, nearly 88 feet tall with a trunk over 3 feet across, standing on the east lawn. It stands beside the Van Cortlandt House Museum, the Bronx.

trees.name: The Great Elm of Central Park West

location.address: Central Park, northeast corner of Central Park West & West 77th Street, New York, NY 10024

trees.transport: 81st Street-Museum of Natural History (Metro B/C), 4 min walk
trees.story:
Central Park once had roughly 500 American elms along its western edge. By 1985, a New York Times survey counted 23 left, and this is one of them. It stands right at the park's edge on Central Park West and 77th Street, directly across from the American Museum of Natural History, wider than it is tall: NYC Parks measures it at just under 51 feet high with a 55 foot canopy.

Dutch elm disease reached New York in the 1930s and worked through the city for decades, killing elms faster than anyone could replant them. This one kept standing while its neighbours came down one by one, close enough to the street that passersby now call it, without much competition, the most beautiful tree on the block.

Nobody has dated it precisely. What is documented is its survival: officially designated one of the city's Great Trees, standing beside a statue of Alexander von Humboldt, who spent his career cataloguing exactly this kind of specimen. No planting record narrows the guess further than a century or more, so that wide range is what the story states rather than a false precise number.

Walk in from the Museum of Natural History subway stop and it is the first tree inside the park, an entrance marker planted long before anyone thought to protect it.
trees.notes: NYC Parks Great Trees register (id=45), corroborated by a dedicated Great Trees blog, a local Upper West Side blog, and Central Park's 2024 Great Trees map update (Westside Rag). Measures 50.84ft tall, 55ft canopy spread. No planting date found anywhere; age given as a wide, honest range rather than a false precise figure. Coordinates are the street intersection, not a surveyed trunk point, so precision is approximate.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by being wider than it is tall, just under 51 feet high with a 55 foot canopy, right at the park's edge. It stands at Central Park West and 77th Street.

trees.name: The Elms on the Rocks

location.address: Rock outcrop just east of the Mall (Literary Walk), Central Park, New York, NY 10022

trees.transport: 72nd Street (Metro B/C), 8 min walk
trees.story:
Two American elms grow straight out of exposed bedrock east of Central Park's Mall, their roots spread flat across the rock like something poured rather than planted. NYC Parks designates them as two separate Great Trees, ids 38 and 39, but they stand close enough on the same outcrop that almost nobody visits one without the other.

The rock underneath predates both trees by a margin that makes their own age beside the point. This is Manhattan schist, some of it dated by geologists at over a billion years old, exposed here by the same nineteenth century landscaping that shaped the rest of the park. The trees carry no planting record of their own, each roughly 78 feet tall, trunks gnarled from decades of finding purchase where there is barely any soil to root in.

What they prove is less about age than persistence. An elm in open parkland can be felled by disease or storm in a season. One growing out of solid rock has already solved a harder problem, and its awkward, rock gripping shape is the visible record of that fight.

They sit a few hundred metres from the Mall's elm allee and about 600 metres from the Ramble, an easy stop on the same walk through the park's oldest plantings.
trees.notes: Two American elms on the same bedrock outcrop, registered separately by NYC Parks (ids 38 and 39) but folded into one entry per the register-twin rule since a visitor sees them as one destination. No planting date for either. Coordinates are the Mall's known reference point rather than a surveyed point for the outcrop itself.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise them by the roots, spread flat across bare rock where there is barely any soil, under two gnarled trunks about 78 feet tall. They stand on the outcrop just east of the Mall.

trees.name: The Elm Allee of Literary Walk
trees.age_estimate: about 100 years (planted in the 1920s, the third planting on this site)

location.address: The Mall (Literary Walk), Central Park, New York, NY 10022

trees.transport: 72nd Street (Metro B/C), 8 min walk
trees.story:
Central Park's most photographed avenue of trees is not the original one. The Mall, also called Literary Walk, has been replanted with American elms twice before the row standing today: the first two plantings failed when foot traffic compacted the soil around the roots, and the elms there now went in during the 1920s, the third attempt, protected from the start by low fencing along the path.

That makes these trees roughly a century old, not the century and a half some press coverage implies by counting from the park's 1858 design. NYC Parks lists the grove as an official Great Tree, and it is often called the largest grove of American elms in the world, a claim the park's own conservancy states more carefully: one of the largest remaining plantations of a species that Dutch elm disease has been cutting down, city-wide, since the 1930s. Central Park still holds about 1,600 elms, several hundred on a rotating fungicide programme, and still loses 15 to 30 a year to the same disease that ended the first two plantings here by other means.

Walk the Mall in full leaf and it reads as a cathedral aisle, two unbroken rows meeting overhead. Every one of them is a replacement, and every one of them is still, by the numbers, worth the trip.
trees.notes: NYC Parks Great Trees register (id=37), Central Park Conservancy's own article, and Untapped Cities' Great Trees guide. Age corrected from press coverage that implies an 1858 planting: the Conservancy states this is the THIRD planting on the site, installed in the 1920s after the first two failed from soil compaction. Superlative softened per hard rule 8: some sources call it the largest American elm grove in the world, the Conservancy's own wording (used here) is 'one of the largest remaining plantations'. Coordinates are the Mall's known reference point, an approximate pin for a promenade rather than one trunk.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the two unbroken rows of elms meeting overhead, low fencing along the path to keep feet off their roots. It stands on the Mall, the avenue also called Literary Walk.

trees.name: The Second Camperdown Elm of Green-Wood
trees.age_estimate: believed 19th or early 20th century planting, exact date unconfirmed

location.address: Green-Wood Cemetery, at the intersection of Garden Path and Pink Avenue, 500 25th Street, Brooklyn, NY 11232

trees.story:
Brooklyn has two Camperdown elms, and genetically they are the same tree. Every Camperdown elm alive is a graft from one contorted branch found on a Scottish estate near Dundee in the 1830s, a mutation that cannot be grown from seed, so each specimen is a cutting of a cutting of that single original. The famous one stands behind the Boathouse in Prospect Park, planted in 1872. This one grows two miles south, inside Green-Wood, where Garden Path meets Pink Avenue.

Nobody wrote down when it went in. New York's Great Trees register named it in 1985 and recorded the species and the corner, not a date, and no later source has supplied one. What the sources do agree on is the order: this is the younger of the two, and old enough to be counted among Green-Wood's landmark trees. A precise year would have to be invented, so there is none here.

The shape carries it anyway. Camperdowns arch their limbs downward and tangle them into one another instead of reaching up, which makes a low dome you duck into rather than stand under, dark inside even at midday. Victorian day-trippers came out to this cemetery in numbers that helped make the public case for Brooklyn's parks, and they came for exactly this: a landscape with curiosities in it. Green-Wood is free and open daily, and the R train stops at the gate.
trees.access: Free, cemetery open daily (check seasonal hours)
trees.transport: 25th Street (Metro R), at the cemetery gate
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by its limbs arching downward and tangling into a low dark dome you duck into rather than stand under. It stands in Green-Wood Cemetery, at Garden Path and Pink Avenue.

trees.name: The Kansas Hawthorn of the Lily Pool

location.address: Brooklyn Botanic Garden, across from the Lily Pool, 990 Washington Avenue, Brooklyn, NY 11225

trees.story:
The largest Kansas hawthorn in the United States grows in Brooklyn, and the species normally gives up at around twenty feet. This one reached 35, on a 20 inch trunk under a 28 foot crown, and in 1985 the American Forestry Association named it a national champion. New York State has carried it on its Big Tree Register since 2009 as one of only two champion trees in the five boroughs. None of that was the plan. Rochester's parks department sent it down as a gift in 1912, and it was planted across from the Lily Pool at the Brooklyn Botanic Garden, which had opened to the public only a year or so before. It has stood there through everything the garden has become since.

Crataegus coccinioides is a hawthorn of the American Midwest, a thorny, unfashionable small tree that most visitors walk past for eleven months of the year. October is the exception, when the leaves go scarlet and orange and the branches hang with dark crimson haws.

Entry to the Garden is paid. The pin here sits at the Washington Avenue gate rather than at the tree, because no survey has recorded its coordinates: walk to the Lily Pool by the conservatory and look for the small tree carrying an unreasonable amount of fruit.

best_time.label: October, when the leaves turn scarlet and the branches hang with dark crimson haws

trees.access: Paid entry to Brooklyn Botanic Garden: adult $22 at the box office (autumn 2026). Open Tuesday to Sunday, 10 a.m. to 6 p.m. in October and to 3:30 p.m. in November; closed Mondays.
trees.transport: Franklin Ave-Botanic Garden (Metro 2/3/4/5) or Prospect Park (B/Q/S), 5-10 min walk
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it in October by the dark crimson haws and scarlet leaves on a small thorny tree, 35 feet up from a trunk 20 inches round. It stands across from the Lily Pool by the conservatory.

trees.name: The Caucasian Wingnut of the Rock Garden

location.address: Brooklyn Botanic Garden, Flatbush Avenue side, just north of the Rock Garden, 990 Washington Avenue, Brooklyn, NY 11225

trees.story:
This tree came from Rome in 1922, and one of its limbs now rests on a crutch. The Caucasian wingnut on the Flatbush Avenue side of the Brooklyn Botanic Garden, just north of the Rock Garden, has grown heavy enough that the garden props and cables its lower branches to stop them tearing out of the trunk. That trunk is the argument: the Garden calls it nearly nine feet through, the city's Great Trees register measures ten, and the two figures have never been reconciled. It stands about 60 feet tall and close to as wide, with roots surfacing in long ridged patterns that run out from the base across the ground.

Pterocarya fraxinifolia comes from the wet forests between the Black Sea and northern Iran and reached European gardens in 1782, which is how an Italian nursery came to have one to send. The name is literal. In midsummer the tree hangs chains of small winged nutlets a foot and a half long from its branch tips, green ropes that stay up, browning, into autumn, and nothing else in the garden does anything like it. A clone of it went in near the Herb Garden in 1978, and the difference in size between the two makes the case for coming to see this one.

Entry to the Garden is paid, and the pin sits at the main gate: the tree is a walk away, along the Flatbush Avenue boundary.

best_time.label: July and August, when foot-and-a-half chains of winged nutlets hang from every branch tip

trees.access: Paid entry to Brooklyn Botanic Garden: adult $22 at the box office (autumn 2026). Open Tuesday to Sunday, 10 a.m. to 6 p.m. in October and to 3:30 p.m. in November; closed Mondays.
trees.transport: Franklin Ave-Botanic Garden (Metro 2/3/4/5) or Prospect Park (B/Q/S), 5-10 min walk
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the props and cables holding its lower limbs up, and in midsummer by chains of winged nutlets a foot and a half long. It stands on the Flatbush Avenue side, north of the Rock Garden.

trees.name: The Cedar of Lebanon Grove near Conservatory Water

location.address: Inside the 72nd Street entrance to Central Park, near Conservatory Water, east side just north of the information kiosk, New York, NY 10021

trees.story: Central Park's own Conservancy calls this a single cedar of Lebanon. A blogger who found the same spot in 2016 counted several, growing together as a small grove, both describing the identical trees just inside the park's 72nd Street entrance, behind the information kiosk near Conservatory Water. Nobody has resolved the discrepancy, and this project would rather say so than guess. What both sources agree on is the plaque at the base, dedicating the planting for grandchildren, a gift from patrons Linda and Mort Janklow, and the species itself: Cedrus libani, the tree on Lebanon's flag and, in the older stories, the timber said to have built Solomon's Temple. It is evergreen where almost everything else in this part of Central Park is not, a pyramidal, blue green shape that holds its form across every season rather than only one. Its cones grow upright on the branch instead of hanging, ripening through autumn into rows that look, from a distance, like eggs balanced along each limb. No planting date survives for this grove; a 2016 estimate guesses a few decades old for Central Park's cedars generally, honest but not a measurement of this specific planting. Conservatory Water sits a five minute walk from three of this walk's other trees, the closest addition this cluster has had.

best_time.label: September to November, when upright cones sit on the branches like rows of eggs

trees.transport: Q train to 72nd Street (Second Avenue), about 10 minute walk west into the park via the 72nd Street/Fifth Avenue entrance

photo.note: Cone close-up identified as Cedrus atlantica, not a readable view of the Lebanon cedar behind the kiosk.

trees.notes: Two independent sources describe evergreen Cedar of Lebanon trees at the same spot, but disagree on count: Central Park Conservancy's own plant page describes 'a beautiful specimen' (singular); gardenindelight.com (2016) describes 'several... in a small grove' at the identical location, with the same dedication plaque. Delivered as a grove/ensemble since the plaque gives one obvious place to stand, per the collectible-point rule. No confirmed planting date; age range is a rough inference from a 2016 blog guess about the park's cedars generally, not a documented figure for this planting, hence the 'not documented' chip label. Coordinates are Conservatory Water's own published centre point (Wikipedia), not a tree-level GPS fix; distance-checked against the existing cluster: roughly 540m to nyc_002, 370m to nyc_012/013, 780m to nyc_011, comfortably within the same walk.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the plaque at the base dedicating the planting for grandchildren, and by evergreen cones that stand upright on the branch. It stands behind the information kiosk inside the 72nd Street entrance.

trees.name: The American Elm at the East 97th Street Entrance

location.address: Central Park, at the East 97th Street entrance, roughly 500 feet west of Fifth Avenue, New York, NY 10029

trees.story: Most of New York's elms are gone. Dutch elm disease arrived in the 1930s and by the postwar decades had killed the overwhelming majority of the American elms that once shaded nearly every street in the city, a loss so total that Central Park's surviving giants now register as minor miracles rather than ordinary trees. This one stands at the park's East 97th Street entrance, its northernmost officially designated Great Tree, an eighty foot canopy spread wide enough to be one of the broadest in the entire register, and a trunk the tree guides describe, not unkindly, as looking like an old witch, its serpentine branches twisting rather than reaching straight up. Nobody recorded when it was planted; city records only say the 1800s, a stretch of a century or more that leaves its exact age an open question. What is documented is what it survived: the fungus that erased its species from most of the city, and, per the park's own account, the storms that have since taken out other Central Park trees around it. New York designated it a Great Tree in 1985, one of the original class, decades before the citywide relaunch that added scores more in 2024. Walk in from Fifth Avenue at 97th Street and it is the first thing waiting.
trees.access: Free, public park, right at a park entrance path
trees.transport: 4/5/6 train to 96th Street/Lexington Avenue, about 10-12 minute walk east and north to the East 97th Street entrance
trees.notes: NYC Parks 'Great Trees of NYC' register (id=46, designated 1985): 94.3 ft tall, 68-inch trunk diameter, 80 ft canopy. Untapped Cities' Great Trees guide independently corroborates the same measurements and calls it the northernmost Great Tree in the park. Westside Rag's 2024-10-09 coverage of the citywide relaunch independently lists the same tree at 94 ft near the East 97th Street entrance. AGE: no source gives a planting year, both that address it say only 'dates to the 1800s' (127-226 years as of 2026), flagged for imprecision rather than disagreement. COORDINATES: nycgovparks.org returns HTTP 405 to direct fetch and web.archive.org was unreachable this pass; coordinates are a good-faith estimate from a geocoded reference point (2 East 90th Street / Engineers' Gate, cross-checked against Nominatim's own East 96th Street result, landing within about 60m), marked approximate rather than tree-level confirmed. DISTANCE: about 170m from nyc_019, 750m from nyc_020, forming a genuine second walk roughly 1.1-1.15km from the existing Ramble/Mall/CPW cluster.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the canopy, eighty feet and one of the broadest on the city's register, and by branches that twist rather than reach straight up. It stands right at the East 97th Street entrance.

trees.name: The London Plane of the Reservoir

location.address: Bridle Path on the east side of the Jacqueline Kennedy Onassis Reservoir, near East 96th Street, Central Park, New York, NY 10029

trees.story: A tree with more than one trunk is hard to age by the usual rule of thumb, and that uncertainty is most of this one's story. The London plane on the Bridle Path near East 96th Street rises just over ninety six feet from a base that splits into multiple trunks fused so thoroughly that its combined diameter tops five feet, bark mottled in patches of green, tan and grey that one NYC Parks writer compared to an impressionist canvas. The claim attached to it, that it was planted around 1862 when the Reservoir beside it was first excavated, comes from one nature writer's educated guess rather than any planting record, which makes 'possibly the oldest tree in Central Park' a title worth repeating with the word possibly intact. A rival candidate exists across the park: a black tupelo in the Ramble that one book on the city's great trees dates to 1858, four years earlier, an argument nobody has settled because neither tree came with a receipt. What is not in dispute is the setting. The Reservoir's running path carries thousands of people past this trunk every week, most looking at the water and the skyline reflected in it rather than down at the multi-trunked plane that has, by the most generous reading, watched the water since before the Civil War.
trees.access: Free, public park, beside the Reservoir's public running/bridle path
trees.transport: 6 train to 96th Street, about 10 minute walk west into the park to the Reservoir's Bridle Path
trees.notes: NYC Parks 'Great Trees of NYC' register (id=43): multi-trunked London plane, Bridle Path near the East 96th Street entrance, northeast corner of the Reservoir, 95.94 ft tall, trunk diameter over 5 ft owing to multiple trunks. Untapped Cities independently corroborates the same tree and measurements, citing nature writer Dennis Burton's claim it was 'possibly planted when the Reservoir was dug' in 1862. A 2026-05-18 Ephemeral New York piece independently repeats the same 1862 dating and measurements, while noting a competing claim that nyc_002 (Black Tupelo of the Ramble) may date to 1858 instead, a dispute between two OTHER trees, not evidence against this one. AGE: 'possibly planted' 1862 is explicitly one writer's guess, not a documented planting record, hence 'not documented' in the chip and flagged status. COORDINATES: same nycgovparks.org access problem as nyc_018; estimate built from the Reservoir's published Wikipedia centroid projected to its northeast corner per the register's own 'near East 96th Street, east side' description, cross-checked against a Nominatim anchor landing within about 60m. Marked approximate. DISTANCE: about 170m from nyc_018, 670m from nyc_020, part of the same second walk.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the base, several trunks fused into one over five feet through, and by bark mottled green, tan and grey. It stands on the Bridle Path by the Reservoir near East 96th Street.

trees.name: The Yoshino Cherries of the Reservoir
trees.age_estimate: not documented; the planting traces to a 1912 gift from Japan

location.address: East side of the Jacqueline Kennedy Onassis Reservoir, near East 87th Street, Central Park, New York, NY 10128

trees.story: Everyone knows Washington's cherry trees came from Japan in 1912. Fewer know New York got a gift the same year: a planting of Yoshino cherries along the Reservoir's east side, sent alongside the 3,020 trees that went to the Tidal Basin and somehow left out of the story that made the capital famous for its blossoms. Thirty five trees stand there today, city designated as a single Great Tree entry rather than thirty five separate ones, which is the honest way to register a planting nobody experiences tree by tree. They bloom white shading to pale pink each April, usually a week or two before the Reservoir's showier Kwanzan cherries on the opposite bank, and the flowers carry a faint almond scent the plum colored Kwanzans do not. Here is the part no one advertises: Yoshino cherries rarely live past sixty years even with good care, and nothing in the historical record says whether the trees blooming today grew from the original 1912 shipment or replaced it at some point since, the way Washington's own planting has been replanted in stages for a century. So the honest claim is not that these particular trunks are old. It is that this exact stretch of path has carried the same seasonal show, on the same imported species, since Woodrow Wilson's first year in the White House.
trees.access: Free, public park, beside the Reservoir's public running path
trees.transport: 4/5/6 train to 86th Street, about 10-12 minute walk west into the park to the Reservoir's east side

best_time.label: mid-April, usually a week or two before the Reservoir's Kwanzan cherries across the water

trees.notes: ENSEMBLE, judged against the collectible-point rule the way nyc_013 (the Mall elm allee) was judged: NYC Parks register (id=42) designates this as ONE 'Great Tree' entry, not many. Untapped Cities independently describes '35 Yoshino cherries... on the east side of the Reservoir', part of the 1912 gift distinct from Washington DC's Tidal Basin planting the same year. Westside Rag's 2024 coverage independently lists '28-foot Yoshino Cherries' at the same location. AGE / OPEN QUESTION: sources agree the SITE traces to 1912 (114 years in 2026), but Yoshino cherries often live only 30-60 years, and no source confirms whether today's 35 trees are original plantings or later replacements, the way DC's Tidal Basin cherries are a mix of survivors and generations of replacements. The honest claim is 'this planting traces to 1912', not 'these are 114-year-old trees'; age range reflects that uncertainty. COORDINATES: same nycgovparks.org access problem as nyc_018/019; estimate built from a Nominatim anchor projected 3 blocks south to East 87th Street, cross-checked within about 60m. Marked approximate. DISTANCE: about 670m from nyc_019, 750m from nyc_018. All three sit within roughly 900m of each other, forming a genuine second walk (about 750m end to end) roughly 1.1-1.15km from the existing Ramble/Mall/CPW cluster.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise them in April by white flowers shading to pale pink, a week or two before the plum coloured Kwanzans on the opposite bank. They stand on the Reservoir's east side near East 87th Street.

trees.name: The Magnolia of Hattie Carthan

location.address: 679 Lafayette Avenue, Bedford-Stuyvesant, Brooklyn

trees.story:
New York has made exactly two trees official landmarks, and this southern magnolia is the only one still standing. The other, the Flushing Weeping Beech, is gone. William Lemken planted this one around 1885 from a seedling brought up from North Carolina, which makes it about 140 years old and a long way from home: Magnolia grandiflora is a tree of the American South, and one flourishing this far north is rare. It has had help. A wing wall on its north side shelters the straight trunk, which the Historic Districts Council puts at over seventy feet.

In 1968 the houses beside it were threatened with demolition and the ground with becoming a parking lot. Hattie Carthan, a Bedford-Stuyvesant resident, formed the Magnolia Tree Committee, local schoolchildren raised money, and on 12 May 1970 the Landmarks Preservation Commission designated the tree an individual landmark. Carthan then founded the Magnolia Tree Earth Center in the brownstone next door. The parking lot never happened; the tree got an institution named after it instead.

Two honest warnings before you go. The building side has been partly hidden by scaffolding for years, so the view from Lafayette Avenue may be less than the tree deserves. And sources disagree on its street number by one, 678 or 679, which is why our pin is approximate. If you have stood in front of it lately, tell us what you could see.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it as the evergreen southern magnolia, its straight trunk over seventy feet tall with a wing wall on its north side. It stands beside the Magnolia Tree Earth Center brownstone on Lafayette Avenue.
trees.access: Free; visible from the public sidewalk on Lafayette Avenue. Stands beside the Magnolia Tree Earth Center brownstone; the garden itself may be closed.
trees.transport: Nearest subway: G at Bedford-Nostrand Avs, about 7 min walk; B44 bus on Nostrand Ave.

best_time.label: June, when it opens its big white flowers

trees.notes:
- NYC Landmarks Preservation Commission designated it an individual landmark 12 May 1970 (LPC report 0957); one of only two trees ever given NYC landmark status, the other (Flushing Weeping Beech) is gone, so this is the only living one.
- Planted c.1885 by William Lemken, grown from a seedling brought from North Carolina; a laurel magnolia flourishing this far north is rare. Age is a documented planting date for THIS specimen (hdc.org says mid-1880s), so 'about 140 years'.
- HDC: straight trunk over seventy feet tall, sheltered by a wing-wall to the north.
- Threatened by demolition/parking lot in 1968; Hattie Carthan formed the Magnolia Tree Committee, schoolchildren raised money; landmarked 1970; she then founded the Magnolia Tree Earth Center in the adjacent brownstone.
- Alive: lifecheck RECENT, iNaturalist obs 2026-08-10 (390024056) at the Wikidata coordinate. Girth not found in sources fetched.
- Pin is the Wikidata/Wikipedia coordinate for the address-level landmark lot, not independently placed on a crown: approximate.
- The LPC PDF downloaded but is a scan, not text-read this pass; its designation date was confirmed via the BBG/HDC/Wikipedia pages.
- Access: view from the street only is my judgement from the descriptions, not a stated source.
- Untapped New York (fetched): the tree 'has been partially obscured by scaffolding for many years' (building side); it gives the address as 678 Lafayette while LPC/HDC/Wikipedia say 679, and the Magnolia Tree Earth Center at 677: address discrepancy of one number, pin stays approximate. Visibility may be poor; the page should say so.

official_register.name: NYC Landmarks Preservation Commission designation report LP-0957 (landmarked 12 May 1977)

trees.name: The Hare Krishna Tree

location.address: Tompkins Square Park, near the curved row of benches at the centre of the park, East Village, Manhattan

trees.story:
On 9 October 1966 a monk from India sat down beneath this American elm and began to chant. A. C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupada and his followers sang the Hare Krishna mantra under it in what is remembered as the first outdoor Hare Krishna chanting in the West, and Allen Ginsberg sang with them. A movement that went on to reach most of the world began its public life here, in the shade of one tree in the East Village. Followers of the faith regard the tree as sacred, and they still come back to it.

NYC Parks counts it among the park's highlights, and a plaque placed in 2001, by most accounts, records the 1966 chanting and mentions the park's venerable American elms. That last detail matters when you arrive, because this is not the only old elm in Tompkins Square. The one you want stands near the centre of the park, by the curved row of benches. Our pin gets you to the right part of the park rather than to the trunk, so let the benches settle it.

Nobody we have read says how old the tree is. It was already big enough to sit under in 1966, and the park itself opened in 1834, but nothing we have found ties this particular elm to the park's early years, so we will not pretend it does. If you know when it was planted, or have put a tape round its trunk, tell us.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by where it stands among the park's several old American elms: by the curved row of benches near the centre of Tompkins Square Park. A Parks plaque records the 1966 chanting.
trees.transport: Nearest subway: L at 1st Ave or 6 at Astor Place, about 10 to 12 min walk; M14A/D bus on Avenue A.
trees.notes:
- An American elm in the park's central plaza, listed by NYC Parks (owner of the ground) as a park highlight; a Parks plaque records that on 9 Oct 1966 A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupada and followers chanted beneath it, the first outdoor Hare Krishna chanting in the West; Allen Ginsberg took part (Wikipedia, search results). Wikipedia: considered sacred to the faith.
- Plaque placed 18 Nov 2001 (Hare Krishna sources via search; not fetched). It notes the park's venerable American elms.
- Alive: Village Preservation says it stands and devotees still return; lifecheck RECENT, iNaturalist 2026-09-27 (403916810) at the Wikidata point.
- Age: no source gives it. It was already a tree in 1966; the park opening in 1834 is NOT evidence for this specimen (bridge trap). Leave age empty and let the page ask.
- nycgovparks.org returns an empty 202 to fetchers, so the Parks highlight page was not read; which elm is meant rests on Village Preservation ('curved row of benches near the centre') and the Wikidata coordinate. Pin approximate. Flagged: location-level evidence thin.

trees.name: The Survivor Tree of the 9/11 Memorial

location.address: National September 11 Memorial plaza, Lower Manhattan

trees.story:
This tree is on the list for what it survived, not for how long it has lived. It is a Callery pear, a species planted along city streets by the thousand, and in October 2001 it was found in the wreckage at Ground Zero with its roots snapped and its branches burned and broken. NYC Parks took it away and nursed it back to health. In 2010 it came home, replanted on the plaza of the National September 11 Memorial, where it stands today among the visitors who come to read the names.

How old it is, nobody has settled, and the accounts do not agree. Some place it in a row of pears planted on the World Trade Center plaza in the 1970s, which would make it about fifty. The New York Public Library's 2020 list of the city's famous trees called it 20 to 25 years old. Neither is a planting record for this tree, so we leave the age open. If you know, tell us.

What the tree does now is give. Every year seedlings grown from it go to communities that have lived through a tragedy of their own; one was dedicated at the New York City Fire Museum on Spring Street in June 2019. At the tree itself the Memorial hands out free weather-resistant tags so you can leave a message on it. Come in April and it is in white blossom.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the message tags visitors leave on it, which the Memorial supplies free at the tree, and in spring by its white pear blossom. It stands on the National September 11 Memorial plaza.
trees.access: Free; the Memorial plaza is open daily 8 a.m. to 8 p.m. per the memorial's own site.
trees.transport: Nearest subway: E at World Trade Center, 1 at Cortlandt St, about 4 min walk.

best_time.label: April, when the survivor flowers white

trees.notes:
- NOT old: an ordinary Callery pear from a row planted on the World Trade Center plaza (search results say 1970s, near Building 5; not on the pages fetched, so treat as unverified and leave age empty). Qualifies on history, not age.
- Fetched and confirmed: found Oct 2001 at Ground Zero severely damaged (snapped roots, burned and broken branches); rehabilitated by NYC Parks (the Fire Museum/nyc.gov page); returned to the Memorial in 2010 (both pages). Search results add the Bronx Arthur Ross nursery and about nine years of recovery, replanted Dec 2010: not on fetched pages, writer should use only found 2001 / returned 2010 unless re-read.
- Seedlings from it are given each year to communities that have suffered tragedy; one dedicated at the NYC Fire Museum, 278 Spring St, 19 Jun 2019 (nyc.gov page).
- Memorial invites visitors to leave messages on free weather-resistant tags at the tree (memorial page).
- Alive: lifecheck RECENT, iNaturalist 2026-08-08 (391980083).
- Wikidata coordinate used; exact spot on the plaza not individually confirmed: approximate. Source is the memorial publishing its own tree plus a city government page.
- AGE SOURCE CONFLICT on what is NOT old: NYPL's 'Ten Famous Trees of NYC' (2020, fetched) says the tree is about 20 to 25 years old; search results said it was one of a row of 1970s plantings (about 50 years). Neither is a dated planting record for this tree: age stays empty.

trees.name: The Ginkgo of the United Order of Tents

location.address: 87 MacDonough Street, Bedford-Stuyvesant, Brooklyn

trees.story:
For almost forty years New York's official list of its Great Trees did not change. In October 2024 NYC Parks finally reopened it, for the first time since 1985, adding 61 trees chosen from more than 270 nominations sent in by the public. This ginkgo in front of a mansion on MacDonough Street was one of them, and the house is the reason people put its name forward.

The mansion belongs to the United Order of Tents, a Black women's fraternal order that has served this community for more than 150 years and is said to have helped people escaping slavery. Coverage of the new list described the ginkgo as holding a piece of that history, which is about the best job description a front-yard tree can have.

What we cannot tell you is how old it is. Ginkgo is one of the longest-lived trees on earth, but that says nothing about this particular one, and no source we have found gives a planting year, a girth or a height. If you have any of the three, tell us: a tree on the city's Great Trees list deserves a number.

The lawn is the Order's, so look from the sidewalk. The Hattie Carthan magnolia on Lafayette Avenue is about a kilometre north-west, which makes the two an easy Bed-Stuy pairing, best in November when the ginkgo turns gold.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it as the ginkgo in front of the United Order of Tents mansion, a house on a wide lot with a lawn with almost 100 feet of frontage. It stands at 87 MacDonough Street; look from the sidewalk.
trees.access: Free; stands in front of the United Order of Tents mansion on a large lot (almost 100 ft of frontage); viewed from the public sidewalk on MacDonough Street. The grounds themselves are the Order's.
trees.transport: Nearest subway: A/C at Utica Ave about 8 min walk, or G at Bedford-Nostrand Avs; about 1 km south-east of the Hattie Carthan Magnolia (nyc_021 area, Lafayette Ave).

best_time.label: November, when the ginkgo turns gold

trees.notes:
- Added to NYC Parks' Great Trees of New York City list on 8 Oct 2024 (first update since 1985; 61 new trees, chosen from 270+ public nominations). The Parks page itself (great-trees?id=86) returns 405 to fetchers, so the designation was read via Brooklyn Paper and BK Reader, which both name this ginkgo; the Parks page title 'Great Trees : Ginkgo' appeared in search results.
- Why it matters per the coverage: it stands beside the mansion of the United Order of Tents, a Black women's fraternal order serving the community for over 150 years (said to have aided people escaping slavery); the tree is described as symbolically holding Black history. History claim is from the news coverage, not checked against the Order's own site.
- No age, girth or height found in any source fetched. Ginkgo is long-lived as a species but nothing says how old THIS tree is: leave age empty and let the page ask.
- Alive: lifecheck RECENT, iNaturalist 2026-04-04 (349897888) at the address node.
- Pin is the OSM address node for no. 87, not a crown: approximate. Wikipedia 87_MacDonough_Street confirms the lot and its lawn but mentions no tree.
- Joins a Bed-Stuy walk with nyc_021's Magnolia, about 1 km away. Lead, not delivered: Red Oak in Saratoga Park (Great Trees 2024, per Brooklyn Paper, 'likely stood since the area served as circus ground'; park centre 40.6850,-73.9190, about 2.3 km east); no tree-level pin.

trees.name: The Dinosaur

location.address: East side of St. Nicholas Avenue, just north of West 163rd Street, Washington Heights, Manhattan

trees.story:
It has been called the largest street tree in Manhattan, and it goes by the Dinosaur. An English elm on an ordinary sidewalk in Washington Heights, it has a trunk about five metres round: the NYC Parks register records a diameter of 60.7 inches. How tall it is depends on whom you ask. The register says 79 feet; Edward Sibley Barnard's book New York City Trees gave it about 110. Nobody has settled it, so we print both.

Its age is in the same state. One writer put it at roughly 230 years in 2008, another at 240 and more, and both think it was probably planted on the estate of what is now the Morris-Jumel Mansion, a couple of blocks south. Call it somewhere between two and three centuries. Rumour goes further and says it stood where George Washington watched a fire in 1776. Even the date of that story is disputed, 21 September or 16 November, so treat it as the rumour it is.

The documented part is the city's regard for it. In 2008 it was one of 25 historic New York trees chosen for cloning, and by 2015 a grafted copy had been planted elsewhere in the city, a spare Dinosaur in case of accidents. It is counted among the few trees left from the days of the Boston Post Road.

The most recent account of it standing that we have found dates from 2021. If you walk past, tell us it is still there.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the trunk, about five metres round, on a plain city sidewalk. It stands on the east side of St. Nicholas Avenue, just north of West 163rd Street.
trees.access: Free; a street tree on a public sidewalk.
trees.transport: Nearest subway: C at 163rd St-Amsterdam Av, about 6 min walk; the Morris-Jumel Mansion is a couple of blocks south.
trees.notes:
- NYC Parks Great Trees register entry (quoted by Barry Popik, and the register is referenced on the Greatest Trees of NYC blog): English elm, 78.72 ft tall, trunk diameter 60.7 in, canopy spread 57.5 ft. 60.7 in diameter = 154 cm, times pi = about 484 cm girth (my conversion). The Gay Recluse (2008) credits Edward Sibley Barnard, New York City Trees (Columbia UP, 2002): about 6 ft diameter and 110 ft tall; Popik also notes Urban Sketchers saying 110 ft. HEIGHT CONFLICT 79 ft (Parks) vs 110 ft (Barnard): deliver both, writer must not pick.
- AGE CONFLICT: Gay Recluse 'roughly 230 years' (as of 2008, so about 245 now); the Greatest Trees blog 'approximately 240+ years'. A search-engine summary said 350 to 450 years; I did not find that on any page I fetched, so it is NOT used. Likely planted on the Morris-Jumel Mansion estate (Popik, Gay Recluse). Band 200-300 is my own broad band around the two sourced figures, not a growth-rate calculation.
- Story: rumoured to have stood where George Washington watched the fire of 21 Sept 1776 (Parks text; Urban Sketchers gives 16 Nov 1776 instead: date disputed, say 'rumoured'). One of few trees surviving from the Boston Post Road era per the blog. Called the largest street tree in Manhattan (Hyperallergic 2021).
- In 2008 it was one of 25 historic NYC trees chosen for cloning by grafting (Gay Recluse); NYT Nov 2015 via Popik: it was grafted and its clone planted elsewhere in the city.
- Aged limbs are supported by steel cables (search summary only, not seen on a fetched page).
- Alive: Hyperallergic 21 Mar 2021 still features it as standing; Gay Recluse 2008. No dated observation from the last two years: lifecheck returned NONE at the geocoded point (the point is approximate, so that is weak evidence). Flagged, writer should say reader confirmation welcome.
- Pin: geocoded segment of West 163rd St; Popik says east side of St Nicholas Ave, Gay Recluse says just north of the eastern corner of 163rd. Not a tree-level coordinate: approximate.
- Stands near an abandoned pharmacy, pre-war apartment buildings and a post-war housing project (2008 description; may have changed).

trees.name: The English Elm of Farragut Lawn

location.address: Farragut Lawn, Madison Square Park, Flatiron, Manhattan

trees.story:
Madison Square Park is probably younger than two of its trees. The park was officially designated in 1847, and the two English elms on Farragut Lawn are believed to be older than that: over 200 years, by the reckoning of the Conservancy that runs the park, which is careful to say believed. When Ignatz Pilat redesigned the park in 1870, he kept them.

That they are still here is the remarkable part. Dutch elm disease is the reason English elms are now rarely planted in the United States, the Conservancy notes, so a pair that has stood through the whole life of the park, in the middle of Manhattan, is rarer than it looks from a lunchtime bench.

In 2023 the Conservancy nominated one of them for NYC Parks' Great Tree Search, and it went onto the city's Great Trees list in 2024. Here is our honest gap: we do not know which of the two it is. They share the lawn at the south end of the park, and nothing we have been able to read says which trunk carries the designation. Our pin marks the lawn, not a tree. If you can tell them apart, or know which one the city listed, tell us and we will point at the right one.

Until then, stand between them. Nobody has published a girth or a height for either, so a tape measure would be welcome too.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise them as the two English elms on Farragut Lawn at the south end of the park; which of the pair is the listed Great Tree is not yet known. Both are believed to be over two centuries old.
trees.transport: Nearest subway: N/R/W at 23rd St, about 3 min walk; 6 at 23rd St.
trees.notes:
- Madison Square Park Conservancy (the park's own manager, publishing its own tree) says two English elms on Farragut Lawn are 'believed to be over 200 years old, dating back to before the park itself was officially designated in 1847', preserved in the 1870 redesign by Ignatz Pilat; the park once had about ten (search summary: only two remain, not on a fetched page). 'As a result of Dutch elm disease, these trees are rarely cultivated in the United States.'
- The Conservancy nominated one for NYC Parks' Great Tree Search 2023; its 2025 Arbor Month report mentions the elm's inclusion in the 2024 Great Trees list. The Parks register page 'English Elm in Madison Square Park' (great-trees/106) appeared in search results; the Parks site 405s fetchers, so the entry itself was not read. Age figure is the Conservancy's 'believed', so keep it vague.
- TWINS: two elms stand on the lawn; the Great Tree is one of them and I could not establish which. Deliver as one point at the lawn; the writer should say two elms stand there. No girth or height found.
- Alive: lifecheck RECENT, iNaturalist 2026-09-15 (400500004) within about 50 m of the lawn point; that proves a tree was photographed there, not which trunk. Conservancy 2025 report treats it as current.
- Pin: Farragut Lawn is the south end of the park; I could not get a tree-level coordinate (Nominatim found no Farragut monument), so the point is my placement on the lawn, park-scale: approximate.
- Lead, not delivered: the James Madison Tree (red oak from Montpelier, planted 1936 for the Madison Avenue centennial, on Sol LeWitt Lawn; 90 years old per the Conservancy; famous but young, collectible on the story only).

trees.name: The English Elm of Fort Greene Park

location.address: Eastern side of Fort Greene Park, along the park's Tree Trail, Fort Greene, Brooklyn

trees.story:
Frederick Law Olmsted and Calvert Vaux are remembered for Central Park and Prospect Park, but some of their planting still stands in Fort Greene. This English elm, according to the coverage of NYC Parks' 2024 Great Trees list, was planted as part of their original design for the park, and the city now counts it among its Great Trees.

The Olmsted and Vaux work here dates from the 1860s, which puts the elm at about 160 years, give or take a couple of decades. Treat that as a derivation rather than a record: nobody has published a planting year for this particular tree, and one writer who went looking called the date simply unknown.

Its size is in a similar state. A blogger who walked the park counted 760 trees, 37 of them elms, and judged this one about 80 feet tall and the largest in the park bar one rival, with a trunk he guessed at ten feet across. That is an eyeball estimate, and it does not match other figures in circulation, so we print no trunk size as fact. If you bring a tape measure, the number is yours to give us.

Look for it on the eastern side of the park, along its Tree Trail; our pin puts you in that half of the park rather than at the trunk.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it as one of the two biggest trees in the park by one count, an English elm about 80 feet tall. It stands on the eastern side of Fort Greene Park, along the park's Tree Trail.
trees.transport: Nearest subway: G at Fulton St or C at Lafayette Av, about 6 to 8 min walk; LIRR/B/Q/R at Atlantic Terminal about 10 min.
trees.notes:
- On NYC Parks' Great Trees list (2024 update): Brooklyn Paper (fetched) says an English elm in Fort Greene Park was 'planted as part of the park's original design' by Olmsted and Vaux. The Parks entry itself (parks/fort-greene-park/facilities/great-trees) and its Tree Trail map return 405 to fetchers and were not read.
- Age is derived from that: Olmsted and Vaux's redesign dates from the 1860s (gothamcanoe says planted perhaps late 1860s, 'unknown planting date'), so about 160 years, broad band; whether THIS elm belongs to that 1860s planting is the paper's claim and the Parks text's, not independently dated. Bridge-claim caution: do not state an exact planting year.
- Size: gothamcanoe (undated blog) eyeballs the trunk at 'perhaps 10 feet' diameter and about 80 ft tall, calling it the largest tree in the park barring one rival, one of 37 elms among 760 trees. A search summary quoted the Parks entry as a 68 in trunk diameter (about 173 cm, girth about 540 cm) and about 80 ft; I could NOT see that number on a fetched page, so it is not recorded as girth_cm. The blogger's 10 ft is an estimate and contradicts it: do not use either as fact.
- Alive: lifecheck RECENT, iNaturalist 2026-08-12 (390691522) in the park's east side; proves a tree photographed there, not which trunk. Park-wide tree removals in the renovation (Wikipedia) are a risk to check; the Parks Great Tree status suggests it is protected.
- Pin: park-level, east side only; no tree-level coordinate found: approximate. Parks Tree Trail map PDF (B032) would place it but is blocked.
- Distance: the Hattie Carthan Magnolia (nyc_021) is about 2.2 km east and the MacDonough ginkgo (nyc_024) about 2.7 km south-east; a Brooklyn day, not one walk. Prospect Park trees (nyc_003, nyc_015, nyc_016) are about 4 km south.
